extraction.methodology_summary: The paper decomposes high-frequency fund returns into a self-inflated component (caused by flow-driven price pressure in concentrated, illiquid underlying holdings) and a fundamental component. Using daily ETF holdings, flows, and stock-level volume and volatility, the authors estimate price impact via pooled OLS regressions with fund-time or fund and time fixed effects. They then examine whether fund flows chase these self-inflated returns by estimating distributed lag return-chasing kernels.

key_findings: Investors chase self-inflated fund returns (price impact) just as much as fundamental returns, indicating they cannot differentiate between managerial skill and price impact.
Self-inflated returns explain 8% of time-series variation in returns for funds that are both large and hold concentrated portfolios.
Flows chasing self-inflated returns predict bubbles in ETFs and subsequent steep drawdowns exceeding 200%.
Every day, ETFs reallocate approximately $500 million of investor wealth due to the price impact of Ponzi flows.
limitations: Timing the crash of bubble ETFs is difficult, as bubble ETFs do not necessarily crash within the first year of the run-up.
